opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are a few things. One way to think about it is that pre-training gets you an enormous amount of data. You take essentially everything people have written, and the model learns from all of it. That's a lot. But it's a strange kind of data, and the model uses it in a way that's quite different from how a person learns.

Evolution, on the other hand, has had an incredibly long time to search for something very specific. It didn't give us knowledge so much as it gave us priors, and maybe more importantly, the learning machinery itself. Look at how a teenager learns to drive. Ten hours, maybe twenty, and they're pretty good. They're not consuming millions of examples. They have this robust value function, this sense of "this feels wrong, I'm too close to that car," and it's there before anyone tells them. Where does that come from? Some of it is clearly something evolution built in.

And it's not only things like vision or locomotion, where you could say evolution had hundreds of millions of years to get it right. Even in domains that didn't exist until recently, like math or programming, people learn with remarkable sample efficiency and robustness. That suggests it's not just a prior about the world. It's something about the learning algorithm being better.

So the question I find myself thinking about is: what is that thing? Pre-training gives you breadth, but the models generalize dramatically worse than people do. You can see it. A model will do amazingly on some evaluation and then make a mistake that a person would never make, or go back and forth between two bugs. That gap in generalization, I think, is one of the most fundamental things. Evolution found some answer to it. We haven't fully found ours yet. But I don't think it's magic. I think it's something that can be understood, and it's one of the most important things to understand.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I think there are a few things going on. One way to think about it is that evolution had a very different kind of optimization problem than the one we solve in pre-training. Pre-training is, in some sense, the simplest thing you can do: you take an enormous amount of data that humans produced, and you ask the model to predict it. And it works astonishingly well, better than anyone had a right to expect. But the thing it's learning is a reflection of the data. It's learning what people wrote down.

Evolution wasn't doing that. Evolution was searching over the learning algorithm itself, over the architecture, over the priors, and it was doing it against the actual world, with the actual consequences of being wrong. If your prior is bad, you don't survive. So the thing evolution produced, the human brain, is a very good learner from a small amount of experience. A child sees a few examples of something and gets it. A teenager learns to drive in ten hours. We don't know how to do that yet. Our systems need orders of magnitude more data to reach a comparable level, and even then the generalization is somewhat weaker and more brittle in ways that are hard to pin down.

So I'd say the edge is this: evolution found the learner, and we found a way to compress the data. Those are not the same thing. Pre-training gives you a kind of knowledge, but it doesn't obviously give you the thing that makes a human sample-efficient and robust. And I think that gap is real, and I don't think it's just a matter of scale. It's possible that the right ideas are missing, and we've been able to avoid noticing because the data was so plentiful. As the data starts to run out, that question becomes much harder to ignore.

astra-6.text:
One reason is that evolution has access to a signal that pre-training may not have. It can select directly for what makes an organism survive and reproduce, and that can produce very specific innate behaviors.

Think about fear. An animal can be afraid of a predator before it has had much experience with one. Somehow, evolution has put into the brain a predisposition to recognize a particular kind of situation and respond to it. And it’s not obvious how that works, because the genome doesn’t get to specify the exact experiences the animal will have.

Pre-training, by comparison, is learning to predict observations. It can learn an enormous amount that way, but evolution is also shaping what the organism cares about and what it is prepared to learn. So that’s a possible advantage. It doesn’t establish that pre-training can’t acquire the same capabilities, but the two processes receive quite different kinds of feedback.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, evolution has access to a different kind of information. Pre-training learns from the data that exists, whereas evolution gets feedback from actually interacting with the world. If an organism has a slightly better way of perceiving or acting, that can affect whether it survives and reproduces.

So evolution can, in principle, discover useful things that are never explicitly represented in text. It can then put those things into the starting point of the organism—its instincts, its architecture, its learning algorithms.

The question is how much of that information can be recovered just from predicting observations. Maybe a great deal. But I don’t think it’s obvious that the two sources of information are equivalent.
